data.overall:
**Executive Summary**

Sequence‑to‑sequence learning for tasks such as machine translation has been dominated for years by recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and, more recently, convolutional models.  Both families suffer from an inherent sequential bottleneck: each time step depends on the previous one, limiting parallelism and inflating training time, especially for long sentences.  Although attention mechanisms have been added to these architectures to capture long‑range dependencies, they have never been used as the sole means of information flow.  The paper therefore asks whether a model can be built that completely discards recurrence and convolution, relying only on attention to relate every token to every other token, and if such a model can be trained efficiently while achieving superior translation quality.

The proposed **Transformer** replaces the traditional encoder‑decoder backbone with stacks of *self‑attention* and *feed‑forward* layers.  Each of the six encoder and six decoder layers contains a multi‑head scaled‑dot‑product attention sub‑layer, a position‑wise fully‑connected feed‑forward network, residual connections, and layer normalization.  Multi‑head attention projects queries, keys and values into eight parallel sub‑spaces (64‑dimensional each) so that the model can attend to different linguistic aspects simultaneously.  Positional information, absent from recurrence, is injected through fixed sinusoidal encodings that enable the network to learn relative positions and to extrapolate to longer sequences.  The architecture is fully parallelizable: all tokens in a batch are processed together, and the computational complexity per layer is \(O(n^{2})\) in sequence length but constant in depth, yielding shorter signal‑propagation paths than recurrent (\(O(n)\)) or convolutional (\(O(n/k)\) or \(O(\log_{k}n)\)) alternatives.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that the Transformer sets new state‑of‑the‑art results on two widely used WMT 2014 translation benchmarks while requiring a fraction of the training budget of prior models.  On English‑to‑German, the large (“big”) configuration reaches **28.4 BLEU**, more than 2 BLEU points above the best published single‑model and ensemble scores, after only **3.5 days** of training on eight P100 GPUs.  On English‑to‑French it attains **41.0 BLEU** (or 41.8 in the abstract) under the same hardware constraints, again surpassing earlier systems that needed weeks of GPU time.  Ablation studies confirm that multi‑head attention, adequate key dimensions, and modest dropout are essential for performance, while learned positional embeddings perform comparably to the sinusoidal scheme.  Beyond translation, a four‑layer Transformer applied to English constituency parsing achieves **F1 = 91.3** (WSJ‑only) and **92.7** (semi‑supervised), rivaling the best published parsers despite being trained on far fewer parameters.

The significance of these findings is twofold.  First, by eliminating recurrence the Transformer unlocks massive parallelism, dramatically reducing training time without sacrificing – indeed, while improving – accuracy; this reshapes the practical economics of large‑scale sequence modeling.  Second, the architecture’s reliance on pure attention yields interpretable attention maps that align with syntactic and semantic structures, suggesting a more transparent way to probe linguistic knowledge in neural models.  The authors anticipate extending the model to non‑text modalities (images, audio, video) and to localized attention schemes that can scale to very long inputs, pointing toward a unified, efficient foundation for a broad class of transduction problems.  The codebase has been released publicly, facilitating rapid adoption and further research.

sections.Abstract:
**Summary of the Abstract**

The paper introduces the Transformer, a neural architecture that replaces recurrent and convolutional components with self‑attention mechanisms, thereby eliminating recurrence and convolutions entirely [Abstract, p. 1]. Experiments on two benchmark machine‑translation tasks demonstrate that the Transformer outperforms existing encoder‑decoder models that use attention, while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less training time [Abstract, p. 1]. Specifically, the model attains 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English‑to‑German task, surpassing the best published results—including ensembles—by over 2 BLEU [Abstract, p. 1]. On the WMT 2014 English‑to‑French task, it sets a new single‑model state‑of‑the‑art BLEU score of 41.8 after only 3.5 days of training on eight GPUs, a fraction of the training cost of leading models in the literature [Abstract, p. 1]. The authors further show that the Transformer generalizes to other domains, successfully applying it to English constituency parsing with both large and limited training data [Abstract, p. 1].
sections.1 Introduction:
**Summary of Section 1 Introduction**

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), including long short‑term memory [13] and gated recurrent [7] variants, are the prevailing techniques for sequence modeling and transduction tasks such as language modeling and machine translation [35, 2, 5] [1 Introduction, p. 2]. Subsequent research has sought to extend the limits of recurrent language models and encoder‑decoder architectures [38, 24, 15] [1 Introduction, p. 2].  

RNNs compute hidden states \(h_t\) sequentially along the positions of the input and output sequences, aligning each position with a computation step. This inherent sequentiality prevents parallelization within a single training example, which becomes a bottleneck for long sequences because memory constraints restrict batching across examples. Although recent work has improved computational efficiency via factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32]—the latter also boosting performance—the fundamental sequential constraint persists [1 Introduction, p. 2].  

Attention mechanisms have emerged as a powerful component in many sequence models, enabling the capture of dependencies regardless of their distance in the input or output [2, 19] [1 Introduction, p. 2]. However, in almost all cases, attention is still combined with a recurrent backbone, with only a few exceptions [27] [1 Introduction, p. 2].  

This paper introduces the **Transformer**, a novel architecture that eliminates recurrence entirely and relies solely on attention to establish global dependencies between input and output. By removing sequential computation, the Transformer permits extensive parallelization and achieves a new state‑of‑the‑art translation quality after just twelve hours of training on eight P100 GPUs [1 Introduction, p. 2].
sections.2 Background: The section explains that reducing sequential computation underlies recent convolution‑based models such as the Extended Neural GPU, ByteNet, and ConvS2S, which compute hidden representations in parallel for all positions but still require a number of operations that grows with the distance between positions (linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet) [2 Background, p. 2]. In contrast, the Transformer achieves a constant‑time relation between any two positions, trading off effective resolution due to attention‑weight averaging—a limitation mitigated by Multi‑Head Attention introduced in section 3.2 [2 Background, p. 2]. Self‑attention (or intra‑attention) is highlighted as a mechanism that relates different positions within a single sequence to produce its representation, and it has proven effective in tasks such as reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment, and learning task‑independent sentence representations [2 Background, p. 2]. End‑to‑end memory networks, which employ a recurrent attention mechanism rather than sequence‑aligned recurrence, also perform well on simple‑language question answering and language modeling [2 Background, p. 2]. Finally, the authors note that the Transformer is, to their knowledge, the first transduction model that relies entirely on self‑attention for both input and output representations, avoiding sequence‑aligned RNNs or convolution altogether, and they outline plans to discuss its advantages over earlier models such as [17, 18] and [9] in subsequent sections [2 Background, p. 2].
sections.3 Model Architecture:
**Summary of Section 3 – Model Architecture**

The Transformer adopts a standard encoder‑decoder framework in which an encoder maps an input sequence \((x_1,\dots ,x_n)\) to continuous representations \(\mathbf{z}\), and a decoder generates an output sequence \((y_1,\dots ,y_m)\) autoregressively, conditioning on previously generated symbols [3 Model Architecture, pp. 2‑4].  

**Encoder and Decoder Stacks**  
Both encoder and decoder consist of \(N=6\) identical layers.  
*Encoder layers* contain a multi‑head self‑attention sub‑layer followed by a position‑wise feed‑forward network; each sub‑layer is wrapped with a residual connection and layer‑normalization, and all sub‑layers output vectors of dimension \(d_{\text{model}}=512\) [3 Model Architecture, pp. 3‑4].  
*Decoder layers* add a third sub‑layer that performs multi‑head attention over the encoder output. The decoder’s self‑attention is masked to prevent a position from attending to future positions, ensuring that the prediction for position \(i\) depends only on positions \(<i\) [3 Model Architecture, pp. 4‑5].

**Attention Mechanisms**  
The core attention function is *Scaled Dot‑Product Attention*: for queries \(Q\), keys \(K\), and values \(V\), the output is  
\[
\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V \tag{1}
\]
[3 Model Architecture, pp. 4‑5].  
Dot‑product attention is preferred over additive attention because it is faster and more space‑efficient, and the scaling factor \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}\) mitigates large dot‑product magnitudes that would otherwise push the softmax into low‑gradient regions [3 Model Architecture, pp. 5].

*Multi‑Head Attention* projects queries, keys, and values \(h=8\) times into lower‑dimensional spaces (\(d_k=d_v=d_{\text{model}}/h=64\)), applies attention in parallel, concatenates the results, and projects back to \(d_{\text{model}}\) [3 Model Architecture, pp. 5‑6]. This allows the model to attend to information from multiple representation subspaces simultaneously [3 Model Architecture, pp. 5‑6].

**Applications of Attention**  
1. *Encoder‑decoder attention*: decoder queries attend to encoder outputs, enabling each decoder position to attend to all input positions [3 Model Architecture, pp. 6].  
2. *Encoder self‑attention*: each encoder position attends to all positions in the previous encoder layer [3 Model Architecture, pp. 6].  
3. *Decoder self‑attention*: each decoder position attends to all preceding decoder positions, with masking to preserve autoregressiveness [3 Model Architecture, pp. 6].

**Position‑wise Feed‑Forward Networks**  
Each layer contains a two‑layer feed‑forward network applied identically to every position:  
\[
\text{FFN}(x)=\max(0,\,xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2 \tag{2}
\]
with input/output dimension \(d_{\text{model}}=512\) and inner dimension \(d_{\text{ff}}=2048\) [3 Model Architecture, pp. 6].

**Embeddings and Softmax**  
Input and output tokens are mapped to \(d_{\text{model}}\)-dimensional embeddings. The same weight matrix is shared between the two embedding layers and the pre‑softmax linear transformation, and embeddings are scaled by \(\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}\) [3 Model Architecture, pp. 6].

**Positional Encoding**  
Because the model lacks recurrence or convolution, positional information is injected via sinusoidal encodings:  
\[
\text{PE}(pos,2i)=\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right),\quad
\text{PE}(pos,2i+1)=\cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)
\]
These encodings allow the model to learn relative positions and potentially extrapolate to longer sequences. Experiments with learned positional embeddings yielded similar results, but the sinusoidal version was chosen for its extrapolation properties [3 Model Architecture, pp. 6].
sections.4 Why Self-Attention:
**Summary of Section 4 – “Why Self‑Attention”**  

The authors compare self‑attention layers with the recurrent and convolutional layers that are traditionally used to map a variable‑length input sequence \((x_1,\dots ,x_n)\) to an output sequence of the same length \((z_1,\dots ,z_n)\). They motivate self‑attention by examining three desiderata: (1) total computational complexity per layer, (2) the degree of parallelizable computation (minimum number of sequential operations), and (3) the path length that signals must traverse to capture long‑range dependencies.  

1. **Computational complexity and parallelism**  
   * A self‑attention layer connects every input–output pair with a constant number of sequential operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires \(O(n)\) sequential operations.  
   * Self‑attention is faster than recurrent layers when the sequence length \(n\) is smaller than the representation dimensionality \(d\), a common situation for sentence‑level models using word‑piece or byte‑pair encodings.  
   * To handle very long sequences, the authors suggest restricting self‑attention to a local window of size \(r\), which would increase the maximum path length to \(O(n/r)\) [4 Why Self‑Attention, p. 6].  

2. **Convolutional alternatives**  
   * A single convolutional layer with kernel width \(k<n\) does not connect all input–output pairs; achieving full connectivity would require a stack of \(O(n/k)\) contiguous‑kernel layers or \(O(\log_k n)\) dilated‑convolution layers, thereby lengthening the longest signal paths.  
   * Convolutional layers are generally more expensive than recurrent layers by a factor of \(k\).  
   * Separable convolutions reduce the complexity to \(O(k\cdot n\cdot d + n\cdot d^2)\). Even when \(k=n\), this complexity equals that of a self‑attention layer plus a point‑wise feed‑forward layer, which is the approach adopted in the authors’ model [4 Why Self‑Attention, pp. 6‑7].  

3. **Interpretability**  
   * The authors note that self‑attention can yield more interpretable models. Inspecting attention distributions shows that individual heads learn distinct tasks, and many heads exhibit behavior related to syntactic and semantic sentence structure [4 Why Self‑Attention, pp. 6‑7].  

In sum, self‑attention offers lower per‑layer complexity (when \(n<d\)), greater parallelism, and shorter dependency paths compared with recurrent and convolutional layers, while also providing interpretable attention patterns.
sections.5 Training:
**Summary of Section 5 – Training**

The authors describe the full training pipeline for their Transformer models.

*Training data and batching*  
- Base models were trained on the WMT 2014 English‑German corpus (~4.5 M sentence pairs) using byte‑pair encoding with a shared 37 k‑token vocabulary [5 Training, p. 7].  
- Big models used the larger WMT 2014 English‑French corpus (36 M sentences) with a 32 k word‑piece vocabulary [5 Training, p. 7].  
- Sentences were grouped by approximate length; each batch contained ~25 k source and ~25 k target tokens [5 Training, p. 7].

*Hardware and schedule*  
- Training ran on a single machine equipped with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs.  
- Base models required ~0.4 s per step and were trained for 100 k steps (≈12 h).  
- Big models took ~1.0 s per step and were trained for 300 k steps (≈3.5 days) [5 Training, p. 7‑8].

*Optimizer*  
- Adam with β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.98, ε = 10⁻⁹ was used.  
- Learning‑rate schedule:  
  \[
  \text{lrate}=d^{-0.5}\,\text{model}\,\min(\text{step\_num}^{-0.5},\,\text{step\_num}\cdot\text{warmup\_steps}^{-1.5})
  \]  
  with warmup_steps = 4000, yielding a linear warm‑up followed by inverse‑square‑root decay [5 Training, p. 8].

*Regularization*  
- **Residual dropout**: dropout applied to each sub‑layer output before addition and normalization, and to the summed embeddings and positional encodings in both encoder and decoder; base model rate Pdrop = 0.1 [5 Training, p. 8].  
- **Label smoothing**: εₗₛ = 0.1 was used, which increases uncertainty (higher perplexity) but improves accuracy and BLEU [5 Training, p. 8].

These training choices underpin the reported performance gains of the Transformer over prior state‑of‑the‑art models.
sections.6 Results:
**Summary of Section 6 – Results**

*Machine Translation*  
- The Transformer (big) model achieved a new state‑of‑the‑art BLEU score of **28.4** on the WMT 2014 English‑to‑German task, outperforming all previously reported single models and ensembles by more than **2.0 BLEU** [6 Results, pp. 8‑9].  
- Training the big model required **3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs**; the base model already surpassed all earlier models and ensembles at a fraction of the training cost [6 Results, pp. 8‑9].  
- On WMT 2014 English‑to‑French, the big model reached **BLEU 41.0**, beating all prior single models while using less than a quarter of the training cost of the previous state‑of‑the‑art; this run employed a dropout rate of **0.1** instead of **0.3** [6 Results, pp. 8‑9].  
- For inference, the authors averaged the last **5 checkpoints** for base models and the last **20 checkpoints** for big models, used **beam size 4** and a length penalty **α = 0.6** [6 Results, pp. 8‑9].  
- The maximum output length was set to **input length + 50**, with early termination when possible [6 Results, pp. 8‑9].  
- Table 2 (not reproduced here) compares translation quality and training costs; FLOPs were estimated by multiplying training time, GPU count, and the sustained single‑precision capacity of each GPU [6 Results, pp. 8‑9].

*Model Variations*  
- To assess architectural components, the authors varied the base Transformer on the English‑to‑German dev set (newstest2013) and reported results in Table 3, using beam search but **no checkpoint averaging** [6 Results, pp. 9‑10].  
- **Row (A)**: Varying the number of attention heads and key/value dimensions while keeping computation constant showed that single‑head attention was **0.9 BLEU worse** than the best setting, and performance degraded with too many heads.  
- **Row (B)**: Reducing the attention key size **dk** hurt model quality, suggesting that compatibility determination is non‑trivial and that a more sophisticated compatibility function than the dot product could help.  
- **Rows (C) & (D)**: Larger models consistently improved performance, and dropout proved effective at preventing over‑fitting.  
- **Row (E)**: Replacing sinusoidal positional encodings with learned positional embeddings yielded nearly identical results to the base model [6 Results, pp. 9‑10].

*English Constituency Parsing*  
- A **4‑layer Transformer** with **dmodel = 1024** was trained on the WSJ portion of the Penn Treebank (~40 K sentences).  
- A semi‑supervised variant incorporated ~17 M high‑confidence sentences from the BerkeleyParser corpus, using a **32 K‑token vocabulary** versus **16 K** for the WSJ‑only setting.  
- Hyperparameters (dropout, attention and residual dropout, learning rate, beam size) were tuned on the Section 22 dev set; all other settings matched the English‑to‑German base translation model.  
- During inference, the maximum output length was increased to **input length + 300**, with a **beam size of 21** and **α = 0.3** for both WSJ‑only and semi‑supervised runs.  
- Results (Table 4) show the Transformer achieving **F1 = 91.3** on WSJ‑only and **F1 = 92.7** semi‑supervised, surpassing all previously reported models except the RNN Grammar [8] [6 Results, p. 10].  
- Notably, the Transformer outperformed the Berkeley‑Parser even when trained solely on the 40 K‑sentence WSJ training set [6 Results, p. 10].

These findings demonstrate that the Transformer delivers state‑of‑the‑art performance on large‑scale machine translation while also generalizing effectively to a structurally constrained parsing task, all with relatively modest training resources.
sections.7 Conclusion:
**Summary of Section 7 – Conclusion**

The authors introduce the Transformer, a sequence‑transduction model that relies solely on attention mechanisms, eliminating the recurrent layers traditionally used in encoder‑decoder architectures [7 Conclusion, p. 10]. They report that, for machine‑translation tasks, the Transformer trains considerably faster than models based on recurrent or convolutional layers and achieves new state‑of‑the‑art results on both WMT 2014 English‑to‑German and English‑to‑French benchmarks. In the German translation task, their best single model surpasses all previously reported ensembles [7 Conclusion, p. 10]. Looking ahead, the authors plan to extend the Transformer to non‑text modalities (images, audio, video) and to explore local, restricted attention mechanisms for handling large inputs and outputs, as well as to reduce the sequential nature of generation [7 Conclusion, p. 10]. The training and evaluation code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/tensorflow/tensor2tensor [7 Conclusion, p. 10].
